title: What Actually Works in Instructional Coaching
author: Zach Groshell
summary: A curation post by Groshell that gathers eight 'Thinking Out Loud' podcast episodes from his series with Gene Tavernetti (Better Teaching: Only Stuff That Works) into a single recurring-themes overview. The premise across the series is to take a concrete problem of practice, name what tends to go wrong, and work toward clearer thinking and more usable actions for teachers, coaches, and leaders. The recurring themes Groshell flags: precision in language, the role of practice and rehearsal as the missing bridge between PD and classroom change, observation that produces insight rather than judgment, coaching structures that reduce friction, and implementation thinking that holds up outside ideal conditions. The episodes range from foundational direct-instruction craft (kickoff, Oct 2024) through coaching-model tradeoffs, observation moves, the dilemma of pulling great teachers into coaching roles, when coaching cycles become bureaucracy, lessons from consulting on what actually moves practice, and how to begin supporting teachers credibly. Groshell positions the series and Tavernetti's mentorship as central to his own development as a coach and consultant.
points: Rehearsal (paired with feedback) is the missing bridge between professional development and actual classroom change; without it, transfer is shaky because teachers only talk about strategies or watch others do them.
Coaching observations are not passive: what you attend to, how you collect evidence, and how you frame what you saw determines whether the debrief becomes helpful or demoralizing.
Best coaching model is context-dependent (full-time vs hybrid, centralized vs distributed) and depends on time, staffing, trust, and leadership clarity rather than on any single template.
Pulling great teachers into coaching can hurt students; great teaching does not automatically equal great coaching, and the staffing dilemma needs explicit pathways rather than assumed promotion.

Implementation lessons from consulting: what leaders think they want often differs from what will actually move practice; alignment and follow-through matter more than the inspiration of a 'big splash' training.
quotes: The 'Thinking Out Loud' episodes on Better Teaching: Only Stuff That Works are a running set of conversations to make sense of instruction, coaching, and implementation as they actually function in schools — not as we wish they did.

The premise is straightforward: Gene Tavernetti and I take a concrete problem of practice, name what tends to go wrong, and work toward clearer thinking and more usable actions for teachers, coaches, and leaders.

We dig into rehearsal as a missing 'bridge' between professional development and actual classroom change. If teachers only talk about strategies (or just watch someone else do them), transfer is shaky. Rehearsal, paired with feedback, helps convert ideas into actions teachers can reliably pull off with students.

We zoom in on what coaches actually do during observations. Observation isn't passive — what you attend to, how you collect evidence, and how you frame what you saw all shape whether the debrief becomes helpful (or demoralizing).

We take on a classic staffing dilemma: pulling great teachers out of classrooms can hurt students, but schools also need credible, skilled coaches. We talk through the opportunity costs, why great teaching doesn't automatically equal great coaching.

Here I reflect on what consulting teaches you about implementation and change: what leaders think they want vs. what will actually move practice, why 'big splash' training often fades, and why alignment and follow-through matter more than inspiration.” Archived from Education Rickshaw on May 1, 2026 by Tim.
